first.rationale: Two directions are live given the situation: promotional pricing (the direct answer to competitor entry pricing) and onboarding simplification (the direct answer to the -4% completion / -6% activation decline). Verification budget goes to the two beliefs that are both decision-critical and weakest against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. memory_73 is the single most consequential and least-supported belief: it is the only justification for matching a competitor on price, and its recorded outcome is 'acquisition and revenue lift' with no retention, margin, or cohort-durability evidence — discount-acquired SMB cohorts are exactly where short-run lift and long-run qualified revenue diverge, so I want the original record before committing the slot. memory_86 is the basis for my intended action, and it too is measured only on proxy outcomes (completion rate, time-to-value, early adoption), not on downstream revenue quality; I need to know whether the original experiment tracked accounts past week one. I deliberately did not spend budget on memory_31 (it is a partially redundant, older corroboration of the same onboarding claim, so verifying memory_86 already tests the shared premise), on memory_57 (referral incentives are off-thesis this week — the deficit is top-of-funnel activation, not expansion within established accounts), or on memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist does not address either declining metric or the SMB price attack). Current intent is simplify_onboarding: it addresses both declining metrics at once, it is supported by two independent inherited records, and unlike discounting it does not purchase volume by degrading the value of the acquired cohort. Flagged downstream risk: cutting required signup fields removes qualification signal, so an activation lift can coexist with a drop in qualified pipeline — the experiment must carry guardrails on lead quality, week-four retention, and revenue per activated account, not just completion rate. If the memory_73 archive shows genuine durable retention data, or the memory_86 archive shows the lift never propagated past early engagement, I will revisit before rollout. Running at standard experiment scale with holdout rather than broad rollout, because the inherited evidence is proxy-metric evidence and the objective is a longer-horizon quantity than anything these records actually measured.

final.rationale: The archive resolved both open questions in the same direction. exp_73 confirms the specific failure mode I was worried about: the 40% SMB discount bought +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue while destroying 30-day retention (-12%), and the original record explicitly instructs against generalizing targeted discounting as a sustainable-growth strategy. The inherited summary of memory_73 ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') had silently dropped the retention collapse and the do-not-generalize caveat, which is exactly the distortion that would have made the competitor's price attack look answerable with a discount. Against the stated objective — sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not this quarter's bookings — promotional_pricing is now ruled out on its own source evidence. exp_86 confirms simplify_onboarding on the dimension that actually mattered: +13% completion, -2.1 days time-to-value, and critically +3% 30-day retention, meaning the lift propagates past the proxy metrics into cohort durability rather than decaying like the discount cohort. So I commit the slot to simplify_onboarding. It is the only candidate that addresses both declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) with a retention-positive record, and it is the structurally correct response to a price attack: competing on time-to-value rather than on price, since a discount war against a better-funded entrant would trade durable revenue for a cohort that does not survive first renewal. Residual uncertainty I am not papering over: memory_31 (signup field reduction) remains unverified and is a different intervention from exp_86's shortened onboarding flow — exp_86 tested flow length, not removal of qualification fields. I therefore scope this experiment to onboarding flow shortening as actually validated, and treat any field-cutting as a separate untested change. Downstream value risk stands: reducing friction can strip qualification signal and shift mix toward lower-intent accounts, so an activation lift can mask a decline in qualified pipeline. Guardrails: holdout control, and read lead quality, 30-day retention, and revenue per activated account alongside completion rate; do not promote to broad rollout on completion-rate movement alone. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout, because exp_86 measured a 30-day window and the objective runs longer than the evidence does. Separately, memory_73 should be rewritten in durable memory to carry the retention loss and the do-not-generalize conclusion, so a future session facing this same competitor pressure does not re-derive the discount from a sanitized summary.
